Editor’s Note: This story has been updated to include comments from an Nvidia spokesperson.

Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) is reportedly asking data-center partners worldwide to restrict how cloud-computing services are sold to Chinese customers, potentially limiting access to advanced AI infrastructure.

Nvidia has introduced new requirements for cloud providers, mandating that at least 51% of their service revenue come from non-Chinese customers, The Financial Times reported Tuesday.

Nvidia’s sales and regional teams communicated the policy verbally instead of issuing written guidance. The rules apply globally, including to data centers outside Asia, and cover new contracts rather than existing leasing agreements, as per the report. Notably, the company previously had no comparable requirement.

Chinese technology companies have relied on overseas cloud leases for demanding artificial-intelligence applications, including training large models. The new restrictions could make that approach more difficult for future projects.

The policy arrives as Washington weighs tighter controls on Chinese access to advanced U.S. chips through overseas cloud providers. Nvidia has also narrowed its approved Asian customer base after conducting stricter compliance reviews.

Nvidia spokesperson told Benzinga, "America cannot win the AI race unless America’s AI infrastructure wins worldwide — if the world’s clouds rely on foreign-made chips, the model and application layers will be foreign-built as well.”

“Datacenters and clouds built on American chips are the foundation that American model and application makers need to compete worldwide. Longstanding U.S. policy encourages every cloud to build on American infrastructure and to win business everywhere they can.”

Read Also: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Was Target of Suspected Chinese Intelligence Asset, Raising Questions Over Potential AI Chip Diversion: Report

China’s Push for AI Chip Independence

U.S. restrictions on high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and chipmaking equipment are limiting China’s advanced AI chip production, but experts warn they could accelerate Beijing’s push for domestic alternatives. UCLA professor Christopher Tang told Benzinga that HBM is the biggest immediate bottleneck, while Nvidia’s share of China’s AI accelerator market has effectively fallen to zero.

Last month, IDC reported that Nvidia held 34% of China’s AI accelerator market in the first half of 2026, compared with Huawei’s 28%, narrowing the gap, as Nvidia shipments fell 44% year-over-year to 678,000 units. IDC did not specify which Nvidia chips were included in its market-share estimate or whether it counted restricted B200 and B300 chips reportedly smuggled into China.

“Memory / HBM” sits at 96%. AMD finance chief Jean Hu warned that high-bandwidth memory and other components remain in tight supply, potentially slowing AI-system shipments.

“Meta” stands at 92%. Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) agreed to deploy up to six gigawatts of AMD GPUs, receiving warrants for up to 160 million AMD shares tied to shipment and other milestones.

“Agentic AI” trades at 90%. AMD unveiled Helion in October, a separate platform for AI agents that execute tasks. Partner-developed configurations are expected this month.

“Microsoft / Azure” stands at 80%. Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) plans to deploy Helios on Azure, with AMD expecting shipments to ramp through the fourth quarter and into 2027.

“Oracle” trades at 71%. Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) announced plans last week to offer cloud services powered by AMD’s next-generation EPYC processors, although no launch date has been disclosed.

What Kalshi Predicts AMD Will Skip

“Export Restriction / Export Control” trades at 23%, despite “China” sitting at 62%. US chip-export rules complicate AMD’s access to the Chinese market.

“TSMC” stands at 20%. AMD relies on TSMC (NYSE:TSM) to manufacture its advanced chips, although Su could discuss capacity constraints without naming the manufacturer.

“Nvidia” trades at just 11%. Despite Nvidia dominating the AI accelerator market, traders expect Su to focus on AMD’s own progress.

Reading the Board

AMD has signed enormous AI deals with OpenAI, Meta and others. Now investors want evidence that those commitments are turning into sales.

Expectations are already high. Jefferies forecasts $17 billion in fourth-quarter revenue, compared with Wall Street’s $16.3 billion consensus.

Simply beating estimates may not be enough. AMD exceeded forecasts in August, yet shares initially fell nearly 9% after hours.

According to Benzinga Pro options data, traders expect a 10.85% move, equivalent to roughly $83 billion in market value at Monday’s closing valuation.

The real test for Su is whether AMD can deliver enough AI revenue to justify investors’ expectations.

Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) stock gained more than 3% on Tuesday as traders moved back into high-beta semiconductor names despite softer index futures.

Nasdaq futures gained 0.74%, while S&P 500 futures were up 0.32% at the time of writing.

Micron’s relative strength comes after a pullback from its mid-year peak, with investors continuing to weigh tight memory supply and AI-driven demand against the risk that future capacity additions eventually create another oversupply cycle.

Memory Supply Remains A Key Driver

Micron remains exposed to strong demand for memory used across AI infrastructure, while industry experts continue to expect supply constraints to persist as manufacturers work to add capacity.

The longer-term debate centers on whether AI demand can continue absorbing new memory production as additional capacity comes online over the next several years.

Cramer Prefers Micron Among Memory Names

Jim Cramer said he prefers Micron over Western Digital Corp. (NASDAQ:WDC), pointing to Micron’s stronger technology position.

Cramer acknowledged on Tuesday that Western Digital had already suffered a significant stock decline and could still fall further, but said Micron would be his preferred name between the two.

His view comes as memory and storage stocks remain volatile despite strong underlying demand from AI infrastructure.

Experts See Shortage Lasting Through 2028 And Beyond

GraniteShares CEO Will Rhind said in July that the Wall Street may still be underestimating how long the high-bandwidth memory shortage can last. He said capacity takes years to add while AI infrastructure spending remains strong, creating a supply imbalance that could persist into 2028.

Yorkville America CEO Steve Neamtz offered a similar view in September, saying new fabs capable of materially easing the shortage may not reach full production until 2028 or 2029. He noted that HBM consumes roughly three times the manufacturing capacity per gigabyte of conventional memory, while demand is also spreading into NAND storage.

Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra has said supply should improve gradually in 2028 but that the company still has no clear visibility on when supply will catch demand. More than 75% of Micron’s 2027 output is already committed.

Investor Ross Gerber said on Oct. 5 that he expects the memory constraint to last even longer, potentially for a decade, as AI infrastructure demand broadens into areas such as robotics. He believes growing end-market demand can absorb new capacity even if component prices eventually decline.

SK Hynix And Samsung Benefit From Tight Supply

Micron’s major DRAM and HBM rivals are also benefiting from the imbalance.

On Oct. 28, Cantor Fitzgerald analyst C.J. Muse expects SK Hynix Inc. (NASDAQ:SKHY) to benefit from AI infrastructure spending, long equipment lead times and tight memory supply through 2030. He highlighted management’s indication that HBM demand is running at roughly twice available supply.

Rosenblatt analyst Kevin Cassidy also expects tight supply to support SK Hynix, citing HBM4 growth, stronger pricing and long-term agreements covering a significant portion of future capacity.

Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. (OTC:SSNLF) has likewise said AI-driven memory demand could make supply constraints even tighter in 2027 than in 2026.

New Supply Remains The Key Risk

The bullish outlook still carries a major risk.

In Sept., Martin Shkreli, who disclosed a short position in Micron, warned that falling memory prices could quickly undermine the earnings cycle.

China’s CXMT is expanding DRAM capacity and preparing to enter NAND, potentially adding more supply over time.

Meanwhile, on Nov. 2, Tastytrade founder Tom Sosnoff said Micron, NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) have not yet declined enough to qualify as oversold after their large rallies, highlighting the disconnect between strong long-term memory fundamentals and continued near-term stock volatility.

Earnings And Analyst Outlook

Micron’s next estimated earnings report is scheduled for Dec. 16, 2026.

Consensus calls for EPS of $35.07, up from $4.78 a year earlier, and revenue of $56.55 billion, compared with $13.64 billion last year.

The stock trades at a 11.2-times P/E multiple.

Pfizer Inc. (NYSE:PFE) on Tuesday reported third-quarter sales of $16.58 billion, beating the consensus of $15.87 billion.

The company said revenues came in ahead of expectations, with strong 7% operational revenue growth in non-COVID products, driven by key brands in the U.S. and select international markets, offset by lower revenues from COVID-19 products.

Pfizer’s adjusted earnings came in at 87 cents per share, beating the consensus of 72 cents.

Revenue Drivers and Non-COVID Portfolio Performance

Total revenue dipped slightly from a year earlier. The operational decrease was driven by lower revenues from COVID-19 products and the Prevnar family, largely offset by higher revenues for Eliquis, Padcev, the Vyndaqel family, Nurtec and Lorbrena.

Excluding contributions from Comirnaty and Paxlovid, revenues for the third quarter grew 7% operationally.

Launched and acquired products contributed $3.8 billion in revenues and grew 32% operationally.

Read Also: Florida Attorney General Sues Pfizer for 'Misleading' COVID-19 Vaccine Safety Claims

Key Drug Sales: Oncology Gains Offset Vaccine Declines

Eliquis (a blood thinner) sales were up 25% to $2.52 billion. Padcev (a cancer drug) sales jumped 55% to $720 million.

Vyndaqel family sales increased 12% to $1.77 billion. Paxlovid sales fell 63% to $449 million, and Comirnaty revenues were $808 million, down 29%.

Prevnar family sales were down 10% to $1.56 billion.

Long-Term Outlook and Pipeline Developments

In earnings prepared remarks, Chairman and CEO Albert Bourla said, “I’m confident Pfizer is well positioned for growth toward the end of the decade and for long-term shareholder value creation. We have line of sight to our aim of delivering a risk-adjusted high-single-digit revenue CAGR from year-end 2028 through year-end 2033.”

Bourla also said, “Our obesity program continued to advance, and recent milestones in oncology, immunology and vaccines further demonstrate the potential of our pipeline. With a robust slate of expected catalysts ahead, I believe we’re well positioned to deliver meaningful new medicines for patients and lasting value in the years ahead.”

Upgraded Full-Year 2026 Guidance

Pfizer raised its fiscal 2026 sales guidance to $62 billion to $64 billion, from $60.5 billion to $62.5 billion, compared with the consensus of $62.17 billion.

The U.S. drug giant raised its 2026 adjusted earnings guidance to $2.95 to $3.05 per share, from $2.80 to $3.00 per share, versus the consensus of $2.96.

Pfizer reported a strong third quarter with 32% operational revenue growth driven by launched and acquired products, along with 7% operational growth in non-COVID products.

The company raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $62-$64 billion and adjusted EPS guidance to $2.95-$3.05, citing strong performance and confidence in executing its strategy.

The company is optimistic about potential high single-digit revenue CAGR from 2028-2033, driven by pipeline products and margin expansion through cost realignment initiatives.

CEO Albert Bourla expressed confidence in the company’s strategic direction and long-term growth prospects, highlighting the importance of pipeline execution and strong commercial capabilities.

OPERATOR

Good day everyone, and welcome to Pfizer’s third quarter 2026 earnings conference call. Today’s call is being recorded. At this time, I would like to turn the call over to Francesca DiMartino, Chief Investor Relations Officer and Senior Vice President. Please go ahead, ma’am.

Francesca DiMartino (Chief Investor Relations Officer and Senior Vice President)

Good morning and welcome to Pfizer’s earnings call. I’m Francesca DiMartino, Chief Investor Relations Officer. On behalf of the Pfizer team, thank you for joining us. This call is being made available via audio webcast. Earlier this morning we released our results for the third quarter 2026 via a press release that is available on our website at pfizer.com. I’m joined today by Dr. Albert Bourla, our chairman and CEO, Cecile Gagan, our CFO, and Chris Boshoff, our Chief Scientific Officer.

After their prepared remarks, we will open the call for questions. Members of our leadership team will be available for the Q&A session. Before we get started, I want to remind you that we will be making forward-looking statements and discussing certain non-GAAP financial measures. I encourage you to read the disclaimers in our slide presentation, the press release we issued this morning, and the disclosures in our SEC filings, which are all available on the IR website on pfizer.com. Forward-looking statements on the call are subject to substantial risks and uncertainty, speak only as of the call’s original date, and we undertake no obligation to update or revise any of the statements.

With that, I will turn the call over to Albert.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

Thank you, Francesca. Good morning everyone, and thank you for joining our call. I’m pleased with another strong quarter for Pfizer. Our excellent commercial execution, including 32% operational revenue growth in the quarter for our launched and acquired products, shows the underlying strength of our business. Financial discipline and ongoing productivity improvement are driving efficiency and contributing favorably toward our margins. And with continued progress of our high-value R&D programs, we believe that we are on a pathway to the next stage of meaningful growth.

Before going further, I want to welcome Cecile Gagan as our Chief Financial Officer. Cecile brings more than 25 years of finance leadership and the proven ability to deliver new sources of growth. She stood out in a global search for her expertise, her deep knowledge of Pfizer and our industry, and a strategic vision that I believe will help Pfizer unlock sustained long-term value for patients and shareholders. I’m looking forward to Cecile’s partnership, and I’m confident she will help us execute with the discipline and ambition this next chapter requires.

Now let me cover several highlights of our progress in this quarter. As you know, over the last few years we have invested close to $80 billion in transactions that have equipped us with key products contributing to current commercial momentum and platforms with transformative potential. About 80% of this investment was for Seagen, Arena, and Biohaven, and we are making good progress in maximizing the value of each one. We are pleased with the overall performance of our acquired products, which grew 37% operationally in this quarter.

Our legacy Seagen portfolio grew 39% year over year in the U.S. in the quarter, driven by the strong performance of Padcev. Bringing Seagen medicines together with the strength and reach of our commercial organization has deepened our presence in the oncology community. We now offer physicians and care teams a broader set of options and more expertise, helping patients and driving growth for Pfizer. Seagen did more than strengthen our commercial position.

It also expanded our ability to discover oncology breakthroughs, doubling the size of our early-stage pipeline at the time we closed the acquisition. In our late-stage development programs, we are advancing potential antibody-drug conjugates that could bring meaningful improvements for patients with cancer. I’m pleased with the pace of progress over the past year with our expansive clinical development program across our obesity portfolio. We plan to advance 10 active and planned Phase 3 trials in 2026, including one evaluating a switch from approved weekly therapies to our investigational monthly GLP-1 peptide, barobenatide. We have made significant progress with enrollment across our pivotal barobenatide program as well as our amylin combination program, where our Phase 2b study is now fully enrolled.

We are working toward the first in a series of potential approvals for barobenatide in 2028, with planning of our go-to-market strategy well underway. Biohaven also has been a strategically important addition for Pfizer. In the quarter, Nurtec grew by 33% operationally, driven by underlying demand and excellent commercial execution. We see real opportunity to help patients with migraine and for the oral CGRP class to be a key growth driver even as we manage market dynamics in a competitive field. We are leading the oral class in the U.S. and are working to extend that position internationally. We are seeing international growth as more patients can now get this treatment in key countries including the UK, Italy, and Japan.

We are also encouraged by strong adoption when we are able to expand access. 2026 execution in R&D has been strong, and we continue to prioritize the highest-value opportunities for patients and future growth across our four therapeutic focus areas. Our excellent progress showcases our momentum in advancing our strategy. In recent months we achieved two key regulatory decisions, one key pivotal readout, and eight key pivotal study starts alongside strong data we presented at several recent medical congresses. We are excited by the pipeline opportunities in areas of strategic focus and commercial strength.

This includes late-stage programs across tumor types in oncology including multiple myeloma, breast cancer, and lung cancer, within inflammation and immunology, and of course in pneumococcal vaccines. Chris will share more detail about our recent advancement in the recent months. Our pipeline strategy is grounded in disciplined prioritization and accelerated execution, and we are confident that we are advancing our most significant opportunities for future patient impact and growth.

Today we are raising our guidance for full-year 2026 revenue and adjusted earnings per share. This reflects our strong performance through the third quarter and confidence in our ability to execute our strategy, along with our financial discipline and the progress we continue to make with our R&D pipeline. We believe Pfizer is well positioned to drive growth towards the end of the decade and create sustained value for patients and shareholders over the long term.

We have deployed AI in our business with the goal of improving efficiency in manufacturing and sharpening how we engage physicians and patients in R&D. We are working to accelerate innovation with faster target validation and better molecule and biomarker selection. The recent launch of Genesys, a new pharmacovigilance platform, shows our commitment to harnessing advanced AI and intelligent automation for global safety monitoring. This typically involves a lengthy manual process for more than 600 products in over 120 countries.

Genesys takes on the administrative burden so our safety scientists can spend their time where it matters most: assessing causality, detecting safety signals, and protecting patients. With that, I will turn it over to Cecile.

Chris Boshoff (Chief Scientific Officer and President, Research & Development)

Thanks, Cecile. Across our four therapeutic areas, we made strong progress last quarter. I’ll provide color on recent developments for some of these programs, starting with Elrexfio, our internally discovered BCMA bispecific, which has now delivered two positive Phase 3 readouts in double-class–exposed multiple myeloma, most recently in MM32. Elrexfio monotherapy demonstrated a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in progression-free survival versus investigator’s choice of three established standard-of-care regimens.

This is important because the choice of three standard-of-care regimens provides a robust representation of how CD38-refractory multiple myeloma is treated today in a patient population that is growing as anti-CD38 therapy moves into the first-line setting, and the results themselves were strong. At the time of the interim analysis, more than 75% of patients receiving Elrexfio had not experienced disease progression or death from any cause, and the estimated 18-month progression-free survival rate was approximately 68%.

Safety in MM32 was consistent with Elrexfio’s known profile and also potentially differentiated, with infection prophylaxis measures incorporated from the start of MM32. Rates of Grade 3 or higher infections were lower than those observed in MM5, Elrexfio’s first positive pivotal trial in double-class–exposed multiple myeloma. For context, such infection prophylaxis measures were not in place at the start of MM5. These were instituted following early deaths due to infections that were concentrated in China and two other countries during the COVID wave, impacting the overall hazard ratio of MM5.

MM5 data are expected at a medical meeting before year-end and will provide further information on efficacy and safety. Taken together, these positive Phase 3 results from MM32 and MM5 strengthen our confidence in moving Elrexfio into earlier lines of treatment. We are building a compelling case of fixed-dose Elrexfio monotherapy from first relapse regardless of prior CD38 exposure, and with additional pivotal studies in newly diagnosed multiple myeloma underway, Elrexfio’s eligible patient population could grow approximately fivefold pending clinical and regulatory success.

Moving next to atirmociclib, our potential first-in-class, highly selective CDK4 inhibitor. Building on the leadership we established with Ibrance, we are advancing atirmociclib as a potential next-generation backbone for first-line and early HR-positive breast cancer. Our KAT6 inhibitor, prevetrostat, is being developed in later-line settings. Atirmociclib was designed in-house to improve upon CDK4/6 inhibitors, the current standard-of-care backbone for HR-positive breast cancer.

A key limitation of this class is safety and tolerability, with CDK6 inhibition being a key contributor to adverse events. We designed atirmociclib to maximize efficacy through greater CDK4 inhibition while improving tolerability by minimizing CDK6 engagement. Atirmociclib is 33 times more selective for CDK4 versus CDK6, comparing favorably versus the standard of care. Here are two data sets fueling enthusiasm for atirmociclib. On the left are data presented at ESMO from the Phase 2 Fallite-1 study of atirmociclib plus fulvestrant in patients with HR-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer. All participants had previously received a CDK4/6 inhibitor, and notably, 92% of atirmociclib participants were randomized within three months of discontinuing a CDK4/6 inhibitor. The atirmociclib regimen reduced the risk of disease progression or death by 40% compared to investigator’s choice fulvestrant or everolimus plus exemestane.

These results in a population with highly refractory or resistant disease increase our confidence in our ongoing Phase 3 trial of atirmociclib versus investigator’s choice of CDK4/6 inhibitor in the first-line setting. On the right are data for atirmociclib’s Phase 2 study in early breast cancer with a combination of atirmociclib plus letrozole: 88% of participants’ tumors demonstrated complete cell-cycle arrest compared to only 18% with letrozole alone.

These results support our plan to combine atirmociclib with a selective estrogen receptor degrader, giredestrant, in a Phase 3 early breast cancer trial expected to initiate within the next few months. This study design has been aligned with regulators, building on the expected approval for giredestrant in this setting. This slide shows Fallite-1 safety and tolerability data alongside results from pivotal studies of the three approved CDK4/6 inhibitors plus fulvestrant. These are cross-trial comparisons; therefore, definitive conclusions cannot be drawn. These data further suggest that high CDK4 selectivity drives improved safety and tolerability, enabling continuous dosing, excellent adherence, and potentially greater efficacy. Grade 3 or higher neutropenia was numerically lower with atirmociclib than with any of the approved agents, with no Grade 4 or 5 neutropenia reported.

Any-grade diarrhea was lower than with abemaciclib and comparable to palbociclib and ribociclib. Dose reductions due to adverse events were 14% with atirmociclib compared to 32% to 43% with the approved agents. Turning to Tivanatomic, we are advancing an extensive program for this potentially best-in-class PD-1/VEGF bispecific antibody, with over 1,200 patients treated globally and a consistent safety profile. This includes two ongoing Phase 3 trials, with two additional Phase 3 trials expected to begin this year. Updated results at ESMO strengthen our confidence as we expand Tivanatomic’s development. Since SITC, confirmed response rates for the pivotal dose of Tivanatomic plus doublet chemotherapy from the ongoing Phase 2 study have risen by roughly 20 percentage points in non-squamous and squamous first-line non-small cell lung cancer.

They now stand at approximately 80%, exceeding those of tislelizumab plus chemotherapy. In this study, median progression-free survival was nearly 14 months for both histologies, an improvement of roughly four to five months versus the comparators. Notably, tislelizumab’s efficacy was consistent with historical Phase 3 results for the leading PD-1 antibody pembrolizumab, which supports the relevance of the control arms. We are also encouraged by how Tivanatomic efficacy and safety results compare with Phase 3 data for the PD-1/VEGF bispecific antibody ivonescimab, while recognizing the limitations of cross-trial comparisons.

Now for TLR-ecramec, a potential first-in-class trispecific antibody. TLR-ecramec was designed in-house to simultaneously target multiple complementary drivers of Type 2 inflammation: IL-4, IL-13, and TSLP. Phase 2 results in atopic dermatitis provide compelling proof of concept. At the top monthly doses, TLR-ecramec treatment led to a placebo-adjusted response rate of about 50% for EASI-75, defined as a 75% or greater improvement in the Eczema Area and Severity Index.

While cross-trial comparisons have limitations, these Phase 2 data suggest the potential for superiority over dupilumab, the current standard-of-care biologic. Key secondary endpoints in our ongoing Phase 3 program are powered to test this hypothesis in a head-to-head setting. For safety, TLR-ecramec demonstrated a favorable profile at subcutaneous doses up to 400 milligrams once every four weeks. The observed frequency of conjunctivitis and injection-site reactions were lower than rates reported with dupilumab and comparable to placebo.

Beyond atopic dermatitis, TLR-ecramec offers a pipeline-in-a-product opportunity, targeting pathways that are validated by approved therapies across nine different diseases. Late-stage studies are underway in severe asthma and moderate to severe COPD. Moving to our potential best-in-class pneumococcal conjugate vaccine program. Building on Prevnar’s 25-plus-year legacy of effectiveness and safety, we are advancing next-generation candidates designed for leading serotype and invasive disease coverage in pediatrics. PCV25 delivered strong Phase 2 results. All 20 serotypes shared with Prevnar 20 met the two-fold post–Dose 4 IgG criterion historically used to establish non-inferiority. Since the pediatric licensure of Prevnar 20 in 2023, the FDA established an updated, more stringent 1.5-fold non-inferiority criterion that is incorporated into our Phase 3 design.

Given the Phase 2 results and tighter confidence intervals expected with a much larger sample size in Phase 3, modeling predicts this criterion will be met for at least 22 of 25 serotypes in our pivotal study. Taken together with sera response data, functional OPA titers, and the totality-of-evidence approach to licensure, these results provide confidence as we aim to deliver a best-in-class pediatric pneumococcal vaccine protecting against serotypes that collectively cause an estimated 84% of invasive disease cases in U.S. children under five.

This would represent an incremental increase of approximately 25 percentage points versus Prevnar 20. Our Phase 3 program is well underway, with the Phase 3 lot-to-lot consistency study already fully enrolled. In adults, PCV35 extends the enhanced serotype 3 technology we validated with PCV25 to other key serotypes, with a Phase 1 start expected this year. Looking ahead, we expect a strong cadence of regulatory decisions, data readouts, and pivotal study starts over the next 12 months. These include a readout from MEFRA1, which, based on the current event rate, is now expected in the first quarter of 2027. If successful, MEFRA1 could support approval for Mefrometastat, our in-house–discovered potential first-in-class EZH2 inhibitor for prostate cancer, expanding our franchise. With that, I’ll hand it back to Albert.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

Thank you, Chris. And in closing, operational excellence is driving commercial momentum across our key growth brands, and I would say, importantly, with our launched and acquired products. Our capital allocation strategy, on the other hand, is designed to create long-term shareholder value, and our late-stage pipeline progress, with a significant number of pivotal readouts expected near term, is strengthening our opportunity to extend our leadership in key areas and make a difference for patients.

I’m confident Pfizer is well positioned for growth towards the end of this decade and for long-term shareholder value creation. We have line of sight to our aim of delivering a risk-adjusted, high single-digit revenue CAGR from year-end 2028 through year-end 2033. Now we will move to Q&A, and operator, please assemble the queue.

OPERATOR

Thank you. If you’d like to ask a question, press star-one on your keypad. To leave the queue at any time, press star. Once again, that is star-one to ask a question. Our first question today will come from Chris Schott with J.P. Morgan. Your line is now open.

Chris Schott (Analyst)

Great, thanks so much for the questions. I just had two pipeline ones. Maybe first on the trispecific TLR-ecramec. How are you thinking about the positioning of this one in atopic derm as we consider, I guess, first-line versus second-line usage, as maybe just think about the very strong data you presented versus a very well-entrenched standard of care? And maybe just a second part of that, just talk about the timelines for the indications beyond AD that you’re pursuing.

The second question was then just pivoting over to the upcoming Phase 1/2a amylin and combo data that we’re going to see here. Can you help set some expectations about how you’re thinking about that data, and then the type of titration schedule that’s being used in that study, just to help us kind of frame out what we’re going to see with that readout? Thanks so much.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

No, thank you. Chris, would you like to cover the timelines of the trispecific and, of course, the amylin and birobenetide questions? And then maybe Alexander, you can speak a little bit about the commercial positioning.

Chris Boshoff (Chief Scientific Officer and President, Research & Development)

Thank you very much for the question. So as you know, we’ve now started the Phase 3 program for torecomyg in atopic dermatitis. Two studies. One of those studies includes a head-to-head against dupilumab. And we also started the Phase 2/3 study, a continuous design for COPD, and Phase 3 studies for severe asthma with expected readouts in 2028 and 2029. Regarding amylin GLP-1, as you’re aware, the SOLIS-1 study is now completely recruited. That is the robustly designed Phase 2b study for amylin single agent and amylin plus barrabenatide in different doses and different titrations. We expect the readout for that study for efficacy in the second half of 2027. The ongoing Phase 1/Phase 2a study will give an update at the end of this year, recognizing that study was designed for safety and PK clinical pharmacology, not for efficacy.

Chris Schott (Analyst)

Thank you. And then what about the positioning of the trispecifics?

OPERATOR

Thank you very much. Next question please. Our next question comes from Dave Risinger with Lyric Partners. Please go ahead.

Dave Risinger (Analyst)

Yes, thanks very much. And I wanted to say congratulations to Cecile on your new role as CFO of Pfizer and look forward to working with you. My question is on U.S. net price in the third quarter and going forward. Could you comment on any gross-to-net benefits to net sales in the third quarter, including from any 340B scrubbing, and discuss U.S. net price prospects looking forward in the near term? Thank you.

Cecile

Thanks very much, first for your good wishes. So as it relates to the pricing in Q3, with the exception of, as we were expecting, the impact on adequate which started in Q3 of the January price decrease, I would say there is not really any very material change in our gross-to-net dynamics during the third quarter. So the performance that we are seeing is for the most part driven by strong market performance and volume rather than dynamics around the gross-to-net.

As we are looking into the future, obviously not commenting today on 2027, but we will reflect into our guidance for 2027 the various dynamics that we are seeing—be it IRA with two of our products entering into the MFP in 2027, and any of the dynamics around the 340B impact and changes, including the credit rebate model implemented starting in January, and also obviously some of the MFN impacts that we have following the agreement we have with the government.

But as a summary, the performance in Q3 is really a reflection of the strong execution rather than dynamics around gross-to-net that would not continue.

OPERATOR

Very well. Thank you very much. Next question please. Our next question comes from Umar Rafat with Evercore ISI. Your line is now open.

Umar Rafat (Analyst)

Hi guys, thanks for taking my question. Albert, there’s clearly been a lot of progress on SG&A improvements over the last couple of years, and I acknowledge that it’s not step function but there’s been improvement. But then I recall Dave, before he moved on, had mentioned that majority of the total net cost savings of 7.2 billion will be delivered by the end of ’26. So when I look now back at the Pfizer P&L, I’m seeing SG&A and R&D was about 24.5 billion back in 2022. It’s about the same in 2026 as well. And I acknowledge R&D has gone up a bit, SG&A has come back a bit, but the broader dynamics on OPEX are still broadly in that $24 to $25 billion camp. And I guess how do you think about that heading into the dividend integrity, the cost lever heading into patent expertise? Thank you.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

Cecile, why don’t you take this question?

Cecile

Yes, so as I mentioned earlier, we are on track to delivering the $7.2 billion of savings that we had implemented as part of our first phase of the cost improvement programs. Those savings were in different places: one in our manufacturing footprint or cost; two in R&D but reinvested, and we are indeed increasing our R&D investment in order to support the pipeline, product and programs that we have in addition to obviously the acquisition that we made; and then on the SG&A side, mostly coming from the commercial and marketing expenses as well as ESG.

So what we are seeing today in our operating expenses—and I would then relate to just the third quarter which had some one-time dynamics that drove the SG&A up—we are still expecting, based on guidance, to see a decline in SG&A versus last year. So that’s the first piece that I would say. Going forward, we have announced our second phase of the program with $2.5 billion of savings both in SG&A and in our cost of manufacturing. Those will translate into savings. So we are expecting to see those translating and mitigating the margin erosion as part of the LOE transition in 2027–2029.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

Thank you very, very much, Yisroel. Next question.

OPERATOR

We’ll go next to Akash Tiwari with Jefferies. Your line is now open.

Akash Tiwari (Analyst)

Hey, thanks so much. Just a couple. I know in the spring you had a kind of 45–50 patient biomarker analysis on your STAT6 and you were going to make a decision on whether to go from stage one to stage two. Is there an update on that program and really how do you think about TARC reduction and biomarker reduction to what we’ve seen with some of the degraders? And then on your GLP-1 amlan, I think your Phase 1/2 you just updated on ClinTrials to 201 patients. I think it was originally planned to be closer to 400. Any color on what drove that decision with the amlin GLP-1 combo with Methra? Thank you.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

Chris. Both questions go to you.

Chris Boshoff (Chief Scientific Officer and President, Research & Development)

Okay, thank you very much. So the first is on STAT6. Potentially first-in-class, oral STAT6 programs. Thanks for the question. This is an area very important for us for the I&I portfolio. As we previously stated, we’ve adapted the program to incorporate some additional DDI studies. So we should give you a readout for the STAT6 later this year. Regarding the amylin and barrabenatide, as I stated earlier, the SOLIS-1 study is fully recruited. That study [is] supporting end of next year and the Phase 1 study was adapted for the additional PK studies we are doing. But there’s really nothing material [that] changes to the trial.

OPERATOR

Thank you. Next question please. We’ll go next to Rommel Devon with Guggenheim. Your line is now open.

Rommel Devon (Analyst)

Great, thanks for taking my questions. Again, maybe on the pipeline one, we noticed that you posted a new Phase 1 trial for your PI3K inhibitor on CT.gov last week. Heard what you said around diptermocyclib and your cat 6. Curious if you can maybe just talk about how you see that asset sort of fitting into your broader breast cancer strategy. And then the other question: maybe coming from ESMO we saw the VULGAR data that AstraZeneca released that could suggest maybe less need for the use of fewer cycles of PADs in patients with bladder cancer. Curious if you have any sort of reactions to that data set or how it might impact how you think the use of PADs may play out in the future.

Chris Boshoff (Chief Scientific Officer and President, Research & Development)

Yes. So firstly on the PI3K, we started a Phase 1 study on an internally discovered PIK3CA inhibitor. Reminder that gedatolosib with Seagen is also a Pfizer-discovered medicine. We have an ongoing clinical trial with Relay with their PIK3CA isoform-selective inhibitor called zobe galasib, and the advantage also in combination with atermaciclib. The advantage of atermaciclib is we do not see DDIs, which has been experienced with all the other CDK4/6 inhibitors combining with the PIK3CA.

So it’s a potentially significant advantage. To your point, up to 40% of ER-positive breast cancer, up to 20–25% of HER2-positive breast cancer will harbor a PIK3CA mutation. So it’s an important area for us. The second question was on the VULGAR data. Just I’ll start briefly. Firstly, this reinforces the use of PADs for muscle-invasive bladder cancer. It reinforces the use of PADs in combination with the PD-1 for muscle-invasive bladder cancer. It also reinforces the confidence we have in the study we’ve just started, 309, which is bladder-sparing PADs pembrolizumab in a bladder-sparing setting, as well as the ongoing planned Phase 3 trial with PADs plus cubonetomib which should also start later this year.

I just want to remind [that] on the VULGAR study this was a no–cisplatin-eligible population. Pathological complete remission was lower than what we’ve seen with pembro plus PADset, which is important, including slightly lower event-free survival. And most importantly, this is a curative-intent setting. So we’re not clear yet which patients can be de-escalated. So that’s important for physicians—who can you actually give less therapy to? Thank you.

OPERATOR

Thank you very much. Next question please. We’ll go next to Evan Segerman with BMO Capital Markets, your line is now open.

Evan Segerman (Analyst)

Hi guys, thank you so much for taking my question. So, Cecile, as you inherit the capital allocation framework kind of established by your predecessor, how do you think about the marginal dollars that you can kind of invest from here between internal R&D, another bolt-on—you talked about BD capacity—deleveraging and eventually restarting buybacks? Where do you currently see the highest respective return for shareholders?

Cecile

Yes. Thanks, Evan. So our priorities are clear and they are not changing versus what was in place. I think we have a solid plan to get us through LOE and post-LOE. So our priorities: invest for growth, maintain or grow our dividend over time, and then keep a strong balance. So through the LOE period, our operating cash flow, financial asset and access to capital market will give us the ability to continue to invest and maintain the dividend as we go.

Post-LOE period, our operating cash flow grows with the levers and we have other options to continue to increase shareholder value. And in that situation, share repurchases become again one of the levers that we have in order to be able to continue [to] enhance that shareholder value.

OPERATOR

Thank you very much. Next question please. We’ll go next to Steve Scala with TD Cowen. Please go ahead.

Steve Scala (Analyst)

Oh, thank you. Two questions. Given the pushout of MEV-PRO 1, were there any changes to MEV-PRO 2 and 3 timelines? So that’s the first question. Second question is for Cecile. So you started at Pfizer when Warner-Lambert was being consolidated, have been through the acquisitions of Pharmacia, Wyeth and Seagen and many BD deals, including that for Eliquis. I think it could be argued that Pfizer’s most successful products have come through deals. And in each of those years, as it is now, Pfizer viewed its pipeline as very good.

So given this history, why doesn’t Pfizer make another big deal its primary focus? Or would you say that the pipeline is significantly better now than at any time in the last 25 years? Thank you.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

Good question. Cecile, what do you think?

Cecile

Thank you. And just for the record, I came with Wyeth and so don’t have the history on all the deals. But I think YSA was one of the best acquisitions that we did and I’ve seen since then a transformation of Pfizer and a strengthening definitely of our pipeline over the last 20, 35 years. So what I would say is, in terms of our priorities, right, we have, as Albert reiterated earlier, invested very significantly over the past few years in key transactions and key acquisitions that are today already kind of like a driving success. We’re talking about petf, we’re talking about Nartech, and we see a lot of opportunities that still remain in the pipeline in cgen, in Medcera, where we have a lot to execute both commercially and on an R&D side and on the commercial side.

So really, as we look at BD going forward and considering our capital allocation priorities, our focus is really on more bolt-on acquisitions that are going to complement the large and rich portfolio that we have in the four therapeutic areas that we’re having. So looking at a BD acquisition is obviously strategically aligned, building upon our expertise and then obviously providing the appropriate financial returns that we would be expecting.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

Thank you, Cecile. Chris, you want to comment a little bit on the timelines of Mevro, and given the interest on the product, maybe Amir also you say a few things about the potential.

Chris Boshoff (Chief Scientific Officer and President, Research & Development)

Thank you very much. I’ll be brief. Since we last spoke about it, the timelines have been updated for Mevro 1 and Mevro 2. A reminder, these are event-driven studies, so it’s based on when we expect events to happen. So Mevro 1 will now read out Q1 2027 and Mevro 2 Q4 2027, and as you’ve seen at ESMO, we’ve got additional data including compelling 8.9 months PFS. Just to correct, Mevro 2 is actually Q4 2027, updated in ClinicalTrials.gov. Thank you.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

And I think Mevro 1 you expect around February.

Chris Boshoff (Chief Scientific Officer and President, Research & Development)

Around February, correct. This is the projections right now based on the way that events are accruing.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

And Amir, why are we so excited about Mevro in terms of the commercial opportunity?

Aamir Malik (Chief U.S. Commercial Officer, Executive VP)

I think three things are probably why we’re excited. One, just remind everybody that our current commercial footprint is anchored in the US alongside Astellas. But Mevro for us is a fully global opportunity in the US and outside the US, so that is very significant and exciting. Second, as Chris mentioned, across Mevro 1, 2 and 3 I think we have the pipeline potential to position Mevro as a multi-indication franchise. So that gives us lots of surface area to compete in.

And finally, if you just think of the total patient populations, we’re talking about over 50,000 in the US, close to 50,000 in the EU4 and UK, another 14,000 in Japan, and 30% of that population could be addressed even with Mevro 1. So there’s a significant patient population, a global opportunity, and clearly an area where we have deep commercial expertise. Those are the things that get us excited about it.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

Thank you, Amir. And, you know, sometimes people forget that Xtandi, which is one of our very big and strong products, we basically have half of the Xtandi in the U.S. and that’s it. Here we are going to have the whole US and the whole global international market. Next question please.

OPERATOR

We’ll go next to Jeff Meacham with Citibank. Please go ahead.

Jeff Meacham (Analyst at Citibank)

Great morning everyone. Thanks so much for the question. Just had two. The first, bigger picture, Albert, from a policy perspective, I know obviously hard to have certainty on, especially given today. But as you look to 2027, what are your thoughts on the potential risks of changes to MFN or perhaps greater scrutiny on the prior OUS agreements? And the second question for Chris on barabenatide. You guys have started a lot of studies across metabolic indications and beyond obesity, diabetes. Want to get your thoughts on expanding barabenatide as a combo strategy into inflammation or neuropsych or even oncology, for example. Obviously the science is really evolving here on the GLP-1 synergies. Thank you.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

And really, thank you, Jeff. On the policy perspectives, clearly policy affects a lot our industry and we are monitoring it very carefully. We are waiting to see what will happen today in the elections. But I think that in any case it looks like we will have a split government, so I don’t think that many things can move legislation-wise. I don’t expect any changes in MFN. I think the agreements are signed and are going until the end of the term of this government, and I expect that there will be a renewed interest in the Congress to investigate several things, but I don’t expect policy changes.

Frankly it’s a very big contrast vis-à-vis what I was telling you a year ago. In 2025 I was really scared about the implications that either tariffs or MFN could have. I think through the successful navigation of those issues we brought the stability that is now projected to last and has brought, I think, this confidence back to the investors to invest in the industry, in our sector. Now with that I will turn it to Chris to comment on the GLP-1 and other things.

Chris Boshoff (Chief Scientific Officer and President, Research & Development)

Yeah, I’ll just quickly start. So our goal is initially to establish barabenatide as a potentially best-in-class, monthly, subcutaneous GLP-1 for obesity. And this is globally. We are starting, as you’ve seen, additional studies now for knee osteoarthritis as well as for obstructive sleep apnea, with or without PAP. And we also will announce additional Phase 3 studies in the coming months in 2027. You’re absolutely correct. We hope to announce some additional studies looking at the backbone of our portfolio, including ionite, potentially in oncology.

URI is an interesting area and you’ll also see the acceleration of Phase 1 programs and current programs that, preclinically, are highly differentiated in this space. Thank you.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

Very good. Next question please.

OPERATOR

We’ll go next to Alex Hammett with Wolfe Research. Your line is open.

Alex Hammett (Analyst at Wolfe Research)

Thank you. Two from me. So as you look at Cywin Bioscience’s GLP-1 launch in China, how are both the obesity and the diabetes markets playing out so far and how is that shaping your thoughts on the commercial opportunity for barobenatide OUS? And then on the Lyme disease vaccine, can you update us on the regulatory path forward following the recent submission in Europe? How are your discussions with FDA progressing and are there any meaningful differences between the FDA and EMA? Thank you.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

I’m not sure I understood the second question.

Alex Hammett (Analyst at Wolfe Research)

Lyme disease. Lyme vaccine.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

Ah, the Lyme vaccine. Okay. Yes. So, Alexander, thank you, Alex, very much. Alexander, maybe you speak a little bit about our GLP-1 in China and what to expect from it.

Alexandre de Germay (Chief International Commercial Officer)

That’s right. So thanks for the question. As you said, Alex, we’ve introduced equaniblutide in China at the end of April of this year and we are satisfied with the way we are progressing. We’re learning a lot through the launch of Penoblutide in China. And the things that we are clearly understanding is there are very different segments within this overall chronic weight management category with patients that are all qualifying for the definition of chronic weight management.

But some of them have more an aesthetic-driven purpose with a very different profile of product that they will be looking for, and their way of acquiring this product is actually very different than on the other, opposite direction, which are very heavy people looking for much more efficacy; tolerability becomes a second point. And so clearly what we are learning is it’s confirming our strategy that if we want to be successful in chronic weight management, you need to have a portfolio, and you need to have a portfolio also because you will need to activate all those different channels and the cost of activation of those channels will be amortized across the portfolio. So those are very, very key confirmations of our strategy.

Now, specifically to ecnoblutide. As you know, we also understood from the get-go that to be successful in chronic weight management in China in particular, you need two things. Of course you need a good profile and we have a very competitive profile. But you also need to have type 2 diabetes because it opens up the hospital channel, but it also opens up, per local regulations, the e-commerce channels. I’m very happy to say that since the end of October we actually got the approval for our type 2 diabetes, which opened up that channel.

Second thing, our competitors have also access to reimbursements. And this is very important to compete effectively. And so I’m also very happy to report that since June we passed the NRDL committees and now we’re expecting the final review by the end of this month so that, hopefully, we can introduce our product into the overall hospital reimbursement system. The combination of those two things will really be the start of our penetration of the market.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

Thank you. And from my perspective, it’s fascinating to see how the commercial model around obesity is so different than anything else and for us reminds us really the times of the Viagra launch, because there are a lot of similarities. People are willing to pay out of pocket for products that they value, irrelevant if they are reimbursed or not. That creates dramatically different size in the international markets. The second was that because of the consumer nature of these launches, the e-commerce and the Internet, as it happened with Viagra that was the first product that was available basically on the Internet, plays a key role. And of course we are pretty much into that space already, rather than if we have already launched an obesity product, because our vaccines and our Paxlovid and our—excuse me—and our migraine products, they really have significant channel through the Pfizer For All, which is our consumer, let’s say, web portal, the website.

So I think we are learning a lot right now in China after we have learned a lot in our Viagra. And to add another dimension, AI is changing the way that promotions are happening right now, and not only at the physicians’ level—actually even more importantly at the patients’ level. So we are learning a lot and we are very happy that we are entering this market because I think it is cut for our capabilities. With that I will ask Chris to comment on the Lyme disease.

Chris Boshoff (Chief Scientific Officer and President, Research & Development)

Thank you for the question. We all know Lyme disease incidence is now—the burden of the disease is increasing globally. The EMA has validated the MAA for Pfizer and Valneva’s Lyme disease vaccine candidate. With the validation, the CHMP will now begin its assessment of the MAA and the CHMP is expected to issue an opinion on marketing authorization 2027. We’ve also now filed in Canada and we continue our discussions with the FDA and should provide an update regarding this in Q4 this year.

Thank you.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

Alexander, any comments here?

Alexandre de Germay (Chief International Commercial Officer)

Yeah, no, I think it’s a very exciting opportunity. Just to remind you that we already have an FSME franchise in Europe and we know how to activate tick-borne populations in those endemic areas because we have a salesforce, we have a commercial play with pharmacies, and so we are very excited with the opportunity. The level of awareness of the population is significantly higher than what we have in FSME. So as we have built these muscles commercially, once we have the approval, we’re very much looking forward for the opportunity to commercialize this vaccine.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

Yeah. And the awareness of the disease, of course, in the US is skyrocketing right now because we do have an increase of severity and incidence. So we are looking forward to concluding the discussion with FDA and submitting our file. Let’s go to the next question please.

OPERATOR

Our next question comes from Michael Yee with UBS. Please go ahead.

Michael Yee (Analyst)

Great, thanks. Maybe two quick pipeline questions for Chris on MedPro. You guys continue to be pretty bullish. I know there was a formulation change to lower the Cmax and improve the tolerability. Maybe you could comment on how you feel about dropouts and the change in formulation to drive your effect and then on to recommend your tri-specific. Again, something you’re pretty bullish on is, can you just comment on neutralizing antibodies or ADAs, things that can be tricky for bispecifics and trispecifics, and how you feel about that.

Thank you.

Chris Boshoff (Chief Scientific Officer and President, Research & Development)

Thank you very much. On the first question on meprometostat, as you pointed out, we did, for the Phase 3 study, adapt to have a more tolerable dose with food where we decrease the Cmax but see similar AUC to what we’ve seen in Phase 1. So we’re very confident in the PK data and the dose that was selected for the Phase 3 study. Regarding tilrigamic, we have not seen functional neutralizing antibodies or functional ADAs thus far. You’re absolutely correct, for any bispecific or trispecific that’s a long-term risk, but so far we haven’t seen anything impacting efficacy and, in fact, longer-term follow-up on the studies we previously demonstrated or showed show us that we do not have an impact on efficacy. So, so far so good with

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

Very good. Let’s keep it that way if you can, please. Next question, please.

OPERATOR

Our final question today comes from Asad Haider with Goldman Sachs. Your line is now open.

Asad Haider (Analyst)

Great. Thanks for taking the question and congrats on the quarter, Cecile, and also many congrats and best of luck to you. A couple for you. First, just on 2027. Appreciate the context provided earlier on price dynamics with respect to IRA and 340B, et cetera, but just any additional high-level qualitative framing on other pushes and pulls next year to be aware of ahead of formal guidance. And how should we be thinking about your guidance philosophy relative to Dave’s broadly speaking?

And then looking out longer term, you are reiterating line of sight to high single-digit revenue CAGR towards the end of the decade off of a 2028 base, as well as citing operating leverage and margin expansion given the cost realignment initiatives. But consensus numbers are not really modeling that. There does seem to be a disconnect on both revenue and the earnings lines versus your own expectations. So as you examined street forecasts, what are the key assumptions that you think are getting most mismodeled in the P&L relative to your own internal expectations as you look out towards that period?

Thank you.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

Cecile. Please make the comments on both.

Cecile

So thanks, Asad, for your question and also for your good wishes. So we’ll provide 2027 guidance around middle of December like we did last year. So I will only for now provide high-level key drivers that we are seeing in 2027. One, obviously the LOE impact not only in the U.S. with Ibrance and Xtandi and some other products, but also in international where we are seeing Eliquis being LOE at the end of 2026. The other thing that I would say is obviously offsetting that is the ramp-up and the launch of our—the ramp-up of our launched and acquired portfolio which, again, as you have seen, is having a very strong performance and NTL opportunity for growth. And then obviously pricing, including MF and IRA, which we will reflect in our guidance.

And then on our cost initiative program that will allow us to continue to, one, invest towards the growth opportunities, the growth drivers that we have on the SINA marketing and commercial space, and then increase the productivity and the growth savings both on the commercial spend and as well on the general and administrative spend. So that’s kind of like the key trends for 2027. But again, more to come as we release guidance later in the year.

As it relates to our high single-digit growth aspiration versus the street, if you look at where that difference is coming from, it’s not really coming from one place or one front product. And so is our growth trajectory either. So what we are seeing as a building block for our growth trajectory—obviously one is the continued growth of our new and acquired product. Not only because the market is still growing, our penetration is still increasing, but also on top of it, we are bringing new indications onto those products in order to be able to continue to address more patient and grow our presence on the market.

The second thing is on the pipeline. So while there are some obvious products that are making a key difference, in our view, versus the street view—obesity being one, some of the oncology products being one—what I will say is our growth trajectory doesn’t rely on one single product or one single therapeutic area. We have a broad portfolio of product, several Phase 3 ongoing as well as upcoming catalysts over the 18 to 24 months, which should give confidence to the outside world also to see the opportunity that we are having in bringing breakthroughs to patients in significant areas of unmet need.

Albert Bourla (Chairman of the Board)

Thank you, Cecile. And I would add that me as a CEO, when I see the difference between our internal projections and the street projections, that of course creates to me the urgency to check our assumptions to make sure that, in light of different opinions from the analysts, we are correct or not. So we have done that repeatedly and we came to the conclusion that we tell you that we expect to have a high single digit from ’28 to ’33 and we know very well where are the discrepancies between the products.

And as Cecile said, they are not only on the pipeline, which many analysts do not cover. So you have the phenomenon that from 12–13 analysts that are forming the overall performance of 2031, for some products only five analysts have this one and the others they don’t. So this is something that is expected in pipeline, but we see also very big discrepancies in already launched new products—that there’s a big difference. I will mention two as just examples that I think people need to reevaluate their assessment. One, it is regarding Nurtec, that we are already close to $2 billion this way if you annualize it, and the street has us almost two and a half by year 2030. So I think there is a discrepancy there. I will also mention another example of the Rex field, where for a competing product the street is forecasting $5 billion and for us $600 million. We aspire to present a profile that is very similar in efficacy and better in tolerability and in side effects.

Now, remains to be proven. But I don’t think the $600 million vis-à-vis $5 billion, it is justifiable even with the current information. So I think that as more information is coming for our pipeline and readouts, I think as more information is coming for the performance actually of the new products—and that includes new launches and acquired products—I think the street probably will start adjusting their numbers and there will be convergence mostly. But with that I think that we come to the end of our call. I want to say that I’m very proud of our performance through the third quarter and the execution, and my thanks goes to my Pfizer colleagues.

As I visit with our people—and I do that in our labs and in manufacturing sites and in markets across the world—I see a team with tremendous talent, dedication, striving for breakthroughs that change patients’ lives. We look forward to sharing additional updates about our progress. And thank you for joining our company call today, and thank you for your interest in Pfizer.

OPERATOR

Thank you. This brings us to the end of today’s meeting. We appreciate your time and participation. You may now disconnect.

Wall Street has spent years paying a premium for companies expected to deliver the fastest growth. Now, one unusual valuation measure suggests that relationship may have flipped. Stocks classified as value are trading at a higher multiple than growth stocks, raising questions about what investors are paying for future earnings.

John Belton, portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds, flagged the shift in recent market commentary. On a 2028 price-to-earnings basis, the Russell 1000 Value Index is now trading at a premium to the Russell 1000 Growth Index. This is the first time that has happened, Belton said, in comments shared with Benzinga over email.

Investors can follow the comparison through the iShares Russell 1000 Value Index Fund (NYSE:IWD) and the iShares Russell 1000 Growth Fund (NYSE:IWF), which track the respective indexes. The 2028 P/E ratio compares current share prices with forecast 2028 earnings, rather than trailing profits, and is not a widely cited valuation measure.

The comparison also does not mean value stocks are more expensive under every metric.

A Strange Shift in Market Leadership

The comparison comes as investors question whether the biggest growth companies can turn heavy investment into returns. Belton said technology companies have delivered strong operating results this earnings season. More than 80% of S&P 500 technology companies beat sales estimates, while roughly 95% topped earnings expectations.

Cloud demand has remained robust.

  • Alphabet Inc.’s (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) Google Cloud grew more than 100%.
  • Microsoft Corp‘s (NASDAQ:MSFT) Azure accelerated for a third consecutive quarter and was guided to accelerate again in the December quarter.
  • Amazon.com Inc (NASDAQ:AMZN) offered an unusually confident outlook for growth of more than 40% in each of the next two years.

Yet all three stocks fell after reporting, Belton noted. That disconnect points to a market focused not just on earnings beats, but on how much companies are spending to sustain growth and when that spending will pay off.

Read Also: QUICK SPARK: Growth Beats Value for the Longest Streak in Stock Market History

Growth Has to Prove Its Price

Hyperscalers reiterated, rather than raised, their capital expenditure outlooks this earnings cycle. Still, investors remain concerned about investment levels and payback periods. Alphabet, Amazon and Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) have turned free-cash-flow negative, while Microsoft remains free-cash-flow positive, according to Belton.

That pressure may help explain why the traditional growth premium is looking less secure. Investors want evidence that AI infrastructure spending can generate durable revenue and profits, rather than simply expand capacity. Belton pointed to Anthropic and OpenAI as examples. These AI-native businesses are demonstrating economic value from the infrastructure buildout, but the market wants more proof, he said.

For investors comparing the two styles, IWD and IWF offer a way to track the respective baskets, but neither ETF is a pure bet on the valuation gap. The unusual 2028 comparison is not, by itself, a signal to abandon growth stocks or chase value.

It is a reminder that a growth label does not guarantee a premium. Investors may be reassessing how much they will pay for earnings that still have to materialize. For growth stocks, the next test may be less about the promise of expansion and more about showing that today’s spending can deliver returns.

Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC) stock gained more than 3% Tuesday morning as semiconductor stocks rebounded from last week’s sharp sell-off, while investors continued to weigh Intel’s weak fourth-quarter outlook against longer-term opportunities in data centers, foundry and advanced packaging.

• Intel stock is gaining positive traction. Why is INTC stock trading higher?

The rebound extended to rivals including Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD), NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU), as traders returned to beaten-down semiconductor names amid stronger technology-sector performance.

Technology stocks rose about 1.6%, while the S&P 500 gained roughly 0.5%.

Weak Guidance Triggered the Sell-off

Intel’s rebound follows a 28.58% plunge Friday after the company issued fourth-quarter guidance well below Wall Street expectations.

Intel had reported third-quarter EPS of 52 cents on revenue of $16.51 billion, topping expectations.

However, management guided fourth-quarter adjusted EPS to 25 cents, versus the 43-cent consensus, and revenue to $15 billion-$16 billion, compared with approximately $17.05 billion expected.

The outlook intensified concerns about weak PC demand and memory-related pressures extending into 2027.

The stock is still up over 65% in 2026 versus AMD’s almost 130%, Micron’s 200% and NVIDIA’s 12%.

Bank of America Moves to the Sidelines

Bank of America Securities analyst Vivek Arya downgraded Intel to Neutral from Buy, arguing the company faces a multi-quarter challenge balancing strong data center growth against weakness in PCs.

Arya said Intel remains more exposed to PCs than data centers, while customers are directing a greater share of IT budgets toward AI infrastructure.

He believes Intel’s manufacturing and foundry strategy is appropriate but said the company must front-load significant capital spending before potentially seeing returns three to five years later.

Arya wants more evidence of external foundry wins and continued data center progress before becoming more constructive.

KeyBanc Sees Long-Term Foundry Upside

KeyBanc Capital Markets analyst John Vinh maintained an Overweight rating while trimming his price target.

Vinh said Intel’s near-term PC outlook remains weak, but he sees the longer-term thesis centered on foundry, advanced packaging and server CPUs.

He expects Intel’s data center business to grow about 60% next year and sees more than $30 billion of external foundry and packaging opportunities by 2030.

Vinh said component demand could decline 25%-30% against an approximately 10% decline in PC units, but he believes foundry and server CPU growth can ultimately offset the weakness.

Moor Insights Remains Constructive On Intel’s Turnaround

Moor Insights & Strategy analyst Patrick Moorhead said Intel’s longer-term foundry thesis remains intact despite the sharp stock decline.

He expects Intel to improve its manufacturing economics in 2027 as server and PC products align more closely with its 18A and 18A-P processes.

Moorhead also expects delayed PC demand eventually to return as memory pricing stabilizes, although he sees a stronger recovery opportunity in 2028, rather than 2027.

Tastytrade Sees Intel as Already Oversold

Tastytrade founder Tom Sosnoff distinguished Intel from Nvidia, AMD and Micron after the sell-off.

He said they had not yet fallen enough to qualify as oversold in his framework and would need declines of roughly 25%-35%.

Intel, by contrast, had already suffered a much deeper reset, leading Sosnoff to view the stock as arguably oversold.

He nevertheless expects a choppy trading environment and cautioned against chasing the first rebound before sellers fully exhaust themselves.

  • Apple Inc (AAPL) is important because AAPL stock had continued to rise during tech stock carnage.  Many investors were simply rushing into AAPL, believing it to be a safe stock.  This morning, AAPL stock is falling after earnings.  Earnings were good, but Apple is seeing margin degradation due to high memory prices.  Some investors who recently bought AAPL, believing it to be a safe stock, are now selling AAPL stock.
  • In our analysis, the most important issue facing Apple is AI agents.  Apple derives significant revenue from its App Store, and the App Store is a strong moat.  AI agents can bypass many apps.  In the conference call, Apple was asked the AI agent question, but Apple failed to respond.  This indicates that the AI agent issue for Apple is real and at this time, Apple does not have a solution.  The issue is especially relevant for us because we are long AAPL from an average of $4.68.  AAPL is a very large position in our portfolio.
  • On the positive side, in our analysis, Apple has a huge opportunity ahead if Apple can get Siri right and find a good solution for AI agents.
  • Palantir Technologies Inc (PLTR) is an important AI software stock.  PLTR stock had been running up during the AI stock carnage.  PLTR reported earnings better than consensus but below whisper numbers.  There are also concerns about deceleration of commercial growth.  PLTR has always derived significant business from the U.S. government.  Bullish investors are betting on commercial growth.  PLTR is in our portfolio, long from an average of $20.15.
  • Midterm elections are today.  Historically, it is a clearing event, and stocks rally irrespective of who wins.  This time, there are two complications:
    • The AI trade is in part dependent upon spending on data centers.  There is rising sentiment against data centers.  Election results may have an impact on data centers.
    • The belief a few days ago that the U.S. would attack Iran after the midterm elections has quickly turned into belief that the U.S. and Iran will strike a deal after the election.
  • Oil is falling as the narrative of a U.S.-Iran deal takes hold.
  • In our analysis, prudent investors need to be careful.  There is no certainty which direction the Iran situation will go.
  • There are important earnings from Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) after hours.  AMD earnings will tell if the PC slowdown is an Intel Corp (INTC) specific problem or if AMD is taking share from Intel.  If the answer is that AMD is taking share from Intel and there is no general slowdown in PCs, it has the potential to reignite the AI trade.
  • Markets always have crosscurrents, both positive and negative.  On this election day, it is important that investors do not get carried away with a bullish or bearish narrative and take time to understand the crosscurrents.  It is also important for investors to not mix their politics with investing.  
  • Even though jobless claims numbers have continued to show a strong employment picture, there is mounting concern about layoffs.  Walt Disney Co (DIS) is planning to achieve 20% cost savings with layoffs.

President Donald Trump said Republicans notched a win in Guam’s governor race and secured a majority in the Guam Senate, calling it a potential signal of momentum heading forward.

Trump said Guam had an "early call" for a Republican victory for governor and congratulated Tony Ada, while also claiming Republicans now hold the Senate. The comments were posted on Truth Social.

“Guam, which has always been considered strongly Democrat, just had an early call for a REPUBLICAN Victory in the top spot, Governor — Congratulations to Tony Ada! Also, the Republicans have the Majority in the State Senate. Wow, hopefully that’s an indication for things to come! President DONALD J. TRUMP,” he wrote.

The State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) and Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) moved higher as Election Day wore on, per Benzinga Pro data, with the S&P 500 rising on a further drop in crude oil prices ahead of midterm results.

The Nasdaq-100 rose 0.6% but still traded in correction territory, down more than 10% from its recent high, according to CNBC.

James Talarico’s Bipartisan Approach

That momentum is echoed in Texas, where Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico expressed a willingness to work with Trump on bipartisan initiatives if elected.

In a Tuesday podcast, Talarico said he would collaborate with Trump on health care, housing and regulatory reforms, viewing it as a chance for a rebirth of Trump’s presidency.

Greg Abbott’s Reelection Odds

In Texas gubernatorial politics, Trump has thrown his support behind Gov. Greg Abbott, endorsing him as an "exceptional Governor."

As of Monday, bettors on Polymarket gave Abbott a 60% chance of winning a record fourth term, though his odds have recently declined from a peak of 95% in July.

Texas Senate Race Tightens

The Texas Senate race remains competitive. In a Thursday interview, Verasight CEO Ben Leff noted that despite markets giving Talarico a 70% chance of victory, the race is closer than many realize.

Polling shows Talarico leading Republican Ken Paxton by a narrow margin, emphasizing the importance of voter turnout.

Scaramucci’s Senate Prediction

On Wednesday, Anthony Scaramucci highlighted the potential for Republicans to maintain control of the Senate, citing Trump’s under-polled support. However, cryptocurrency markets disagree, giving Democrats a 67% chance of winning both chambers of Congress.

Prediction Markets Favor Democrats

As of Tuesday, prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket expect Democrats to gain control of the Senate with at least 53 seats. The markets give Democrats a 74% chance of winning the Senate, reflecting a potential shift in political power.
